content: The fourth edition of the guidelines incorporates the first and second addenda, focusing on the probabilities of infection among pathogens and hosts. For further details, refer to the supporting document Hazard Characterization for Pathogens in Food and Water (Annex 1). This assumption is valid for low-risk scenarios, such as those discussed here. Not all infected individuals will develop clinical illness, as asymptomatic infections are common for most pathogens. The percentage of infected individuals who develop clinical illness depends on the pathogen and other factors, such as the host's immune status. The annual risk of illness is determined by multiplying the probability of infection by the probability of illness given infection. For example, a risk of 2 × 10⁻⁴ per year indicates that, on average, one out of 4,600 consumers would contract campylobacteriosis from drinking water. The disease burden per case varies significantly. For instance, in low-income regions, 1,000 cases of rotavirus diarrhea result in 480 disability-adjusted life years (DALYs), whereas in high-income regions, the burden is only 14 DALYs per 1,000 cases due to better access to healthcare. This disparity in disease burden necessitates stricter water treatment requirements in low-income regions to achieve the same level of risk (expressed as DALYs per person per year). Risk assessments should be adapted to specific national contexts, as some pathogens, such as Cryptosporidium in immunocompromised individuals, may be more significant in certain countries. Immunity developed after an initial infection can provide lifelong protection for some pathogens, such as hepatitis A and rotaviruses. In developed countries, where the proportion of young children in the population is lower, only 6% of the population is susceptible. Uncertainty in risk outcomes arises from variability and gaps in the data collected during risk assessments. Ideally, risk assessment models should account for this variability and uncertainty, but the current discussion presents only point estimates. Producing more comprehensive data would require significant time and resources but would improve understanding of raw water quality and treatment performance. The degree of treatment required depends on variables such as daily water consumption and the fraction of the population susceptible to infection. For example, in developed countries, a significant proportion of the population over five years old may not be immune to rotavirus illness. Variations in the susceptible fraction of the population can significantly impact risk estimates. Health outcome targets should guide water safety plans and interventions at community and household levels. These targets aim to achieve measurable disease reductions in the population. For instance, a water quality intervention resulting in a health gain of more than 5% would be considered highly valuable in many parts of the world. Demonstrating health gains, such as reduced E. coli counts at the point of consumption, can be a powerful tool for incremental improvements in drinking water safety. Pathogen occurrence in source waters is critical for selecting high-quality water sources, determining pathogen concentrations, and establishing treatment requirements to meet health-based targets. However, resource limitations often necessitate alternative approaches, such as using sanitary surveys and indicator testing. Pathogen concentrations in wastewater and raw water vary widely due to factors such as population size, dilution with industrial wastewater, and shedding patterns. Conventional wastewater treatment typically reduces microbial concentrations by one to two orders of magnitude before discharge into surface waters. However, untreated or partially treated wastewater may still contribute to pathogen loads in source waters. Pathogen inactivation, die-off, and sedimentation also play roles in reducing concentrations, but these factors vary with the water body and climate. Treatment processes for drinking water often involve multiple stages, such as coagulation, flocculation, sedimentation, filtration, and disinfection. The effectiveness of treatment depends on factors such as water quality, operational conditions, and interactions between treatment steps. For example, failure in one step, such as coagulation, can reduce the efficacy of subsequent disinfection processes. Household water treatment technologies can also play a role in improving water quality, particularly in settings without centralized treatment systems. These technologies include methods such as chlorination, UV disinfection, and filtration, which can effectively reduce microbial contamination when properly implemented.
